question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Analia ends up controlling everything. Once Analia's Lay Claim resolves attached to Corrupted Conscience, Analia controls Corrupted Conscience, and because Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature," that control-changing effect now works for its new controller — so Analia also controls Bane Alley Blackguard (which Analia owns anyway). Nico controls nothing here afterward.

Why: an Aura's controller is tracked separately from the controller of the thing it's attached to, and changing control of one doesn't change control of the other ([303.4e]). Lay Claim doesn't change control of Bane Alley Blackguard directly; it only takes Corrupted Conscience ([Lay Claim ruling #0] — gaining control of a permanent doesn't drag along Auras attached to it, and an Aura's "you" refers to its own controller). But Corrupted Conscience's own text is a continuous control effect keyed to "you," i.e., whoever currently controls Corrupted Conscience ([303.4m], [110.2b]); with Analia now that player, the grant of control over Bane Alley Blackguard flows to Analia. Bane Alley Blackguard still has infect from Corrupted Conscience, and it does not become newly "summoning sick" in a way that resets — it simply changes controller, so Analia can't attack with it this turn unless it has haste or has been under Analia's control since their turn began.

Also note Corrupted Conscience remains attached to Bane Alley Blackguard; nothing about the Lay Claim resolution moves it ([303.4j]). Analia is the controller of Lay Claim itself, attached to Corrupted Conscience.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that if a control effect ends and the default controller has left the game, the object is exiled ([800.4c]).

answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a 4/4 Legendary Enchantment Creature — God.

Assumption: Alan's devotion to red and white is less than seven (they told us devotion to white is 2, and nothing suggests enough red symbols to reach seven combined). Devotion to red and white = the number of mana symbols among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls that are red, white, or both (CR 700.5, 700.5a). If it were actually seven or more, Iroas would already be a creature on its own — but the answer is the same either way, as shown below.

Why: Alan now controls five enchantments (Iroas, God of Victory, the 3 others, and Starfield of Nyx), so Starfield of Nyx's static ability turns on. Both of the relevant effects are type-changing effects applied in layer 4 (CR 613.1, 613.1d), applied in timestamp order:
- Timestamp 1 — Iroas, God of Victory's own ability: while devotion to red and white is less than seven, it isn't a creature (removes the creature type; it stays a Legendary Enchantment — God, and CR 205.4b/205.1b keep its supertype and other types).
- Timestamp 2 — Starfield of Nyx: each other non-Aura enchantment Alan controls "is a creature in addition to its other types," re-adding the creature type. Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment other than Starfield of Nyx, so it qualifies.

Since Starfield of Nyx's effect has the later timestamp, it wins in layer 4, and Iroas, God of Victory ends up an Enchantment Creature. (No dependency applies here under the layer rules; it's straight timestamp order.)

Then in layer 7b, Starfield of Nyx sets base power and toughness each equal to mana value. Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W}, mana value 4, so it is 4/4 — its printed 7/4 is overwritten by the base-setting effect (CR 613.6 covers one ability applying parts in multiple layers, layer 4 and layer 7b here). Nothing here changes its abilities, so it keeps indestructible, granting menace, and the damage prevention.

Multiplayer note: none of this depends on the number of players — devotion counts only permanents Alan controls, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up 5/4.

Why: characteristics are worked out in layers (CR 613.1g, 613.5).

Layer 6 (abilities): Crowd's Favor grants Grizzly Bears first strike (timestamp: when Crowd's Favor resolved). Archetype of Courage, controlled by Amia (Nathanael's opponent), has the later timestamp and says creatures Nathanael controls lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike. Applied after Crowd's Favor, it strips first strike off Grizzly Bears, so in layer 6 Grizzly Bears ends with no abilities at all. Note that Crowd's Favor's power-boost part still applies even though its ability-granting part has been undone — CR 613.6 says an effect applies each part in its own layer.

Layer 7c (power/toughness modifiers): Grizzly Bears' base 2/2 is modified by Muraganda Petroglyphs ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2"), which now applies because Grizzly Bears has no abilities after layer 6, and by Crowd's Favor's +1/+0. Order within 7c is by timestamp (CR 613.4c, 613.7), but since both are additive the result is the same: 2/2 → 4/4 → 5/4.

Timing assumption: Crowd's Favor fully resolved before Archetype of Courage was cast, as stated. If instead Archetype of Courage were already on the battlefield when Crowd's Favor resolved, the result would be identical — Grizzly Bears could never gain first strike ("can't have or gain first strike"), so it would still be 5/4.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the player count. Archetype of Courage affects "creatures your opponents control," so at a table with more than two players it strips first strike from every opponent's creatures, and Muraganda Petroglyphs likewise affects all creatures with no abilities regardless of controller.

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:

It keeps its card types and supertypes — it's still a nonbasic land (CR 205.4c; Murmuring Bosk ruling #0), and it loses its {T}: Add {W} or {B} ability and its enters-tapped text.

question: Alfred controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
Alfred's Saproling token ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a nonbasic land with the land type Mountain (not Forest), and it can tap for {R}.

How you get there: both Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") are type-changing effects applied in layer 4 [613.1d]. Within a layer, effects normally apply in timestamp order, but dependency overrides timestamps [613.7, 613.8]. Blood Moon is dependent on Life and Limb here: on its own, Blood Moon does nothing to a Saproling token, because the token isn't a land until Life and Limb makes it one. So Life and Limb is applied first, then Blood Moon.

1. Start with the token as created: a 1/1 green Saproling creature.
2. Life and Limb (layer 4) makes it a creature and a land, with the creature type Saproling and the land type Forest, in addition to its other types; Forest stays a land type and Saproling stays a creature type [Life and Limb ruling #3, 205.1b].
3. Blood Moon (layer 4) now sees a nonbasic land and makes it a Mountain, replacing the Forest land type with Mountain (it doesn't touch the creature type Saproling, and supertypes are unaffected by card-type/subtype changes [205.4b]). As a Mountain it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}." Effects are applied once in this ordering; Life and Limb does not then re-apply to turn it back into a Forest [613.6].
4. Layer 7 gives it power and toughness 1/1 from Life and Limb [613.1g].

Practical consequences: it's a land, so it can be tapped for {R}, it's subject to summoning sickness as a creature, and land-destruction/creature-destruction both hit it. Note it is not a Forest, so Life and Limb's Forest clause and any "Forest" searching won't find it.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

One caveat grounded outside the provided text: the exact rule that a land type replaces other land types and grants the corresponding mana ability isn't included in the context above, so that part rests on Blood Moon's own text saying nonbasic lands *are* Mountains.

question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
answer:
Both end up identical: a 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Saproling with only the ability "{T}: Add {R}."

How we get there. Both Life and Limb and Blood Moon are type-changing effects applied in layer 4 (CR 613.1d), in timestamp order (CR 613.7): Life and Limb entered first, Blood Moon second. Each effect changes what the other applies to, so they depend on each other and the dependency system can't break the tie (CR 613.8); timestamp order governs.

Layer 4, first Life and Limb: Sapseep Forest is a Forest, so it becomes a Saproling creature and keeps its other types (Land — Forest Saproling; CR 205.1b, 205.3c, Life and Limb ruling #3). The Saproling token becomes a Forest land in addition to being a creature (Life and Limb ruling #1).

Layer 4, then Blood Moon: both objects are now nonbasic lands, so Blood Moon sets their land subtype to Mountain. Per CR 305.7 and Blood Moon ruling #2, each loses the land type Forest and all abilities from its rules text and old land types, and gains "{T}: Add {R}." Setting a land's subtype removes no card types or creature types, so both stay Creature and stay Saproling. Sapseep Forest therefore loses its "This land enters tapped" and "{G}, {T}: You gain 1 life" abilities, and it never has Life and Limb's granted "{T}: Add {G}" (Life and Limb ruling #2) because Blood Moon's later layer‑4 change strips the Forest type that would grant it.

Layer 5: Life and Limb still makes them green — CR 613.6 keeps each part of Life and Limb's effect applying in its own layer to the same objects even though they're no longer Forests by then.

Layer 7b: Life and Limb sets power and toughness to 1/1.

So: Sapseep Forest = 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, "{T}: Add {R}"; the token = the same. Both are subject to summoning sickness as creatures. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Assumed timing: the stated entry order (Life and Limb, then Blood Moon, then Sapseep Forest, then the token) sets the timestamps. If Blood Moon had entered before Life and Limb, Blood Moon would apply first — Sapseep Forest would be a Mountain, not a Forest, so Life and Limb wouldn't turn it into a Saproling creature at all (though the Saproling token would still become a Forest land, then not be re-Mountain'd by the earlier Blood Moon in that same layer pass).

question: Ainsley controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], a [Cinder Glade], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Cinder Glade and Saproling look like?
answer:
Direct answer: Cinder Glade is just a nonbasic Land — Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}" (not a creature). The Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling Creature Land — Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}" (no green mana ability).

Why, layer by layer (both effects are type-changing effects in layer 4, CR 613.6):

Cinder Glade: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Cinder Glade has no "basic" supertype, so it's nonbasic (CR 205.4c). Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types, its rules-text abilities, and gives it the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.7, 305.6, Blood Moon ruling #2). So it loses Forest, loses "{T}: Add {G}", and loses "This land enters tapped unless you control two or more basic lands." Because it is no longer a Forest, Life and Limb — which only affects Forests and Saprolings — never applies to it at all. (Blood Moon is applied first here both by timestamp and because Life and Limb's applicability depends on it, CR 613.8a-style dependency.)

Saproling token: Life and Limb makes all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types (CR 205.1b, 205.3c; Life and Limb ruling #3 — Forest is the land type, Saproling the creature type). That makes the token a Forest land with no "basic" supertype, i.e. a nonbasic land, which is now something Blood Moon applies to. So Blood Moon is applied after Life and Limb here (its effect on the token exists only because Life and Limb applied). Blood Moon sets its land subtype to Mountain: it loses Forest and the {G} ability and gains "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.7). Setting a land's subtype doesn't remove card types or creature types (CR 305.7, 205.4b), so it keeps Creature and Land and keeps Saproling; Life and Limb's color and 1/1 parts still apply in layers 5 and 7b (CR 613.6). Result: a 1/1 green Saproling Creature Land — Mountain, subject to summoning sickness, and it can only be played as a land if it were ever a card (CR 305.9 — irrelevant for a token on the battlefield).

Note a loop-ish consequence: it is Life and Limb that made the token a Forest, and Blood Moon's dependent application then removes the Forest type — but under CR 613.6 Life and Limb's other parts keep applying, and the type-adding part still applied first, so the outcome above is stable.

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since both enchantments affect all matching permanents regardless of controller.

question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Ore-Rich Stalactite ends up as a green artifact land creature — Forest Saproling, a 2/2, that still has its own abilities plus "{T}: Add {G}."

How it gets there, layer by layer (613.1d, 613.6):

- Layer 4 (types): Ore-Rich Stalactite starts as a noncreature Artifact. March of the Machines makes it an artifact creature. Xenograft then makes it a Saproling in addition to its other types. Because it is now a Saproling, Life and Limb applies to it and makes it a Saproling creature and a Forest land in addition to its other types. (Life and Limb entered earlier, but its effect can only apply once Xenograft has made Ore-Rich Stalactite a Saproling; the dependency rules themselves weren't included in the context here, but the end state is the same either way once you re-check the effects.) Result: card types Artifact, Land, Creature, with subtypes Forest (land type) and Saproling (creature type) — each subtype correlating to its own card type (205.3c, 205.1b, 205.2b, 300.2, 205.3i, 305.5). Life and Limb adds the Forest type rather than setting the subtype in a way that strips text, and adding land types leaves existing rules text and types intact (305.7), so Ore-Rich Stalactite keeps "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell" and its Craft ability. It also has no supertypes added — it is not basic (205.4b).
- Layer 5 (color): Life and Limb makes Ore-Rich Stalactite green; it is a green permanent (it was already red-indicated only on its back face, which is irrelevant while the front face is up).
- Layer 6 (abilities): Having the Forest land type grants the intrinsic "{T}: Add {G}" (305.6, Mountain entry shows the same pattern for basic land types).
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): Two effects set power and toughness — March of the Machines sets it to its mana value (2/2) and Life and Limb sets it to 1/1. These are applied in timestamp order, and March of the Machines entered after Life and Limb, so March of the Machines wins: Ore-Rich Stalactite is 2/2.

Practical notes: it's subject to summoning sickness for attacking and for {T} abilities until Alannah has controlled it continuously since her most recent turn began. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming all four permanents are on the battlefield simultaneously now, entering in the stated order. If, say, Xenograft had entered before March of the Machines, the type outcome would be identical but the layer 7b timestamp comparison is unchanged since only March of the Machines and Life and Limb set P/T.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?
answer:
Both lands are colorless nonbasic lands with the single land subtype Mountain and only the ability "{T}: Add {R}" — even though Humility has stripped Magus of the Moon's abilities.

Why: Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Magus of the Moon is a creature, so Humility does remove its "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" ability — but only in layer 6 (ability-adding/removing). Continuous effects are applied in the layer order of CR 613.1, and Magus of the Moon's land-type-changing effect is applied earlier, in layer 4 (type-changing). Once an effect has started to apply, CR 613.6 keeps it applying in every later layer even though the ability generating it has been removed. So the type change sticks.

Result for Furycalm Snarl: a colorless nonbasic Land with subtype Mountain. It loses its printed "As this land enters..." ability and its printed "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" (Magus of the Moon's effect sets the land's types and, as a land-type-changing effect, replaces its old land abilities), and by CR 305.6/107.4a it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}". Note per Furycalm Snarl ruling #1 it had no land subtypes of its own before this.

Result for Crosis's Catacombs: identical — a colorless nonbasic Land with subtype Mountain (it loses Lair), no enters-the-battlefield sacrifice ability, no "{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}", just "{T}: Add {R}" from CR 305.6.

Neither is a basic land: they lack the "basic" supertype, and CR 205.4c says a land without that supertype is nonbasic even if it has a basic land type — which is also why Magus of the Moon keeps applying to them.

Magus of the Moon itself is, thanks to Humility, a 1/1 creature with no abilities; the entry order you gave (Humility before Magus of the Moon) doesn't change the outcome here, because layer order, not timestamp, decides this — timestamps only matter within a layer, and these two effects are in different layers.

This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on opponents.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 blue Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn" plus its own "{2}: Discard a card").

Why Yixlid Jailer doesn't stop it:

1. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That is an ability-removal effect (rule 113.10). Rule 612.3 states that effects which add or remove abilities do not change the text of the objects they affect. So Mistform Skyreaver, while in Aiden's graveyard, still has its printed text — it simply has no functioning abilities as a graveyard card.
2. Volrath's Shapeshifter is not a copy effect and does not "gain Mistform Skyreaver's abilities." Its static ability gives it the *full text* of the top creature card. Rule 612.6 covers exactly this card: "full text" changes not just the text box and type line but also the text representing name, mana cost, color indicator, power, and toughness. Because it operates on text, and Yixlid Jailer's effect doesn't alter text (612.3), Volrath's Shapeshifter reads Mistform Skyreaver's printed text — including Flying — and gets it.
3. The condition is still met: Mistform Skyreaver is still a creature card in the graveyard. Yixlid Jailer removes abilities, not card types, and "Creature — Illusion" comes from the type line, not from an ability.
4. Per Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1, it keeps the granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability in addition to the text it takes on; per ruling #4, no "enters" abilities of Mistform Skyreaver trigger from the change.

Timing note: this is a static, continuously-checked condition. The moment Mistform Skyreaver stops being the top card of Aiden's graveyard (or stops being a creature card), Volrath's Shapeshifter reverts to a 0/1 blue Phyrexian Shapeshifter with just "{2}: Discard a card" (ruling #0).

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents; it works identically in two-player and multiplayer games. Note also that Yixlid Jailer affects cards in *all* graveyards, so any opponent's graveyard cards are likewise stripped of abilities without their text changing.

question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?
answer:
No. Nickolas can't tap Dryad Arbor for {G}, because Dryad Arbor no longer has that ability at all.

Why: Dryad Arbor is a Land Creature — Forest Dryad, and its mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" is printed on it (it has no basic-land-type mana ability of its own beyond that). Overwhelming Splendor says "Creatures enchanted player controls lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Since Dryad Arbor is a creature Nickolas controls, applying the continuous effects in CR 613 order gives: layer 6 — all abilities removed; layer 7b — base P/T set to 1/1. Result: a green 1/1 Land Creature — Forest Dryad with no abilities. With no mana ability to activate, there is nothing to activate; you can't activate an ability that doesn't exist (CR 602.1, 602.2).

Note the second sentence of Overwhelming Splendor — "Enchanted player can't activate abilities that aren't mana abilities or loyalty abilities" — is not what stops Nickolas here; that clause would actually permit mana abilities (CR 113.4, 605.3a). The ability is gone via the first sentence, so the permission is moot. Also note that the ability being unusable wouldn't matter for classification anyway: a mana ability stays a mana ability even when it can't produce mana (CR 605.2) — but here it isn't merely unusable, it's removed.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Overwhelming Splendor is already on the battlefield attached to Nickolas and Dryad Arbor is already on the battlefield, as stated. If instead Nickolas taps Dryad Arbor for {G} in response to Overwhelming Splendor (while it's still on the stack), the mana ability resolves immediately without using the stack (CR 605.3b, 405.6c) and he gets his {G} before the Aura ever applies. And per Overwhelming Splendor ruling #5, if some effect grants Dryad Arbor a mana ability *after* Overwhelming Splendor is attached, that new ability isn't removed and could be activated.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table: Overwhelming Splendor enchants one specific player, Nickolas, and only affects creatures that player controls, so other players' Dryad Arbors are unaffected.

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
Both Swab Goblin and Watchwolf become copies of Figure of Destiny as printed — not the 8/8 Avatar version.

Why: Mirrorweave's copy effect gives them Figure of Destiny's copiable values, which are derived from its printed text as modified only by copy effects, face-down status, and "as ... enters" P/T-setting abilities. The pumped-up state from activating Figure of Destiny's abilities is a type-changing/P-T-setting continuous effect, not a copiable value, so it is not copied (CR 707.2, 707.2a; see the Chimeric Staff example in 707.2). Copying happens in layer 1a (CR 613.2a), so all other continuous effects still apply on top afterward, and the copy change doesn't remove noncopy effects already affecting the permanent (CR 707.4).

Swab Goblin: named Figure of Destiny, a red-and-white (from the {R/W} hybrid mana cost) Creature — Kithkin with base power/toughness 1/1 and all three of Figure of Destiny's activated abilities. Pack's Favor's +3/+3 was already applying and keeps applying in layer 7c (CR 707.4, 613.7), so it is a 4/4. Aspen can activate the copied abilities anew (they start over from the first one, since this permanent isn't a Spirit or Warrior yet).

Watchwolf: named Figure of Destiny, red and white, but Lignify is still attached and keeps applying above layer 1 — layer 4 makes it a Treefolk (that's its only creature type now; it's still a Creature card type), layer 6 makes it lose all abilities (so it does not have Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities), and layer 7b sets base power and toughness to 0/4. Result: a red-and-white Creature — Treefolk named Figure of Destiny, 0/4, with no abilities. Lignify's ruling confirms it overwrites even characteristic-defining power/toughness and creature-type abilities.

Timing assumption: Pack's Favor resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, as stated. If instead Mirrorweave resolved first and Pack's Favor afterward, the result would be identical here — layer 7c always applies after the layer-1a copy, so Swab Goblin is 4/4 either way.

Figure of Destiny itself is unaffected (Mirrorweave says "each other creature") and remains the 8/8 Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar with flying and first strike. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game since Mirrorweave only affects creatures per its own text and no defending-player or per-opponent choice is involved.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao ends up as a black Goblin Zombie creature, 4/2 — yes, it gets +1/+1 from Dralnu's Crusade.

Why: both Conspiracy and Dralnu's Crusade have type-changing parts that apply in layer 4 (CR 613.1d). Conspiracy sets the creature types of creatures Allison controls to the chosen type, Goblin, replacing all other creature types (CR 205.1a; Conspiracy ruling #4), so Leopard-Spotted Jiao loses Beast. Dralnu's Crusade's part is 'All Goblins ... are Zombies in addition to their other creature types,' which only adds (CR 205.1b).

Order within layer 4 is normally timestamp (Dralnu's Crusade is older), but this is a dependency: applying Conspiracy changes what Dralnu's Crusade applies to (it makes Leopard-Spotted Jiao a Goblin), and neither effect is a characteristic-defining ability, so Dralnu's Crusade depends on Conspiracy and is applied after it (CR 613.8a). Result in layer 4: Goblin, then Goblin Zombie.

The rest of Dralnu's Crusade then applies to it too, since it's now a Goblin: layer 5 makes it black only (not black in addition to red — Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0), and layer 7c gives +1/+1, taking base 3/1 to 4/2 (CR 613.6, 613.5).

Timing note: this is the state once Conspiracy has resolved and is on the battlefield with Goblin chosen. Before Conspiracy resolves, Leopard-Spotted Jiao is just a red 3/1 Beast and gets nothing from Dralnu's Crusade.

Player count doesn't matter here: both cards only care about creatures Allison controls / all Goblins, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant is 4/4 (and is a Shapeshifter Zombie Elemental).

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library," so when Duplicant's imprint ability exiles Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, its three +1/+1 counters go with it to the exile zone. This card text overrides the normal rule that counters cease to exist when a permanent changes zones.

A +1/+1 counter on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield adds to that object's power and toughness [122.1a], and the Skullbriar ruling confirms this explicitly (a Skullbriar in the command zone with a +1/+1 counter is 2/2) [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]. So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 1/1 plus three +1/+1 counters = 4/4 in exile.

Duplicant's static ability then gives Duplicant "the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it." That's a setting effect applied in layer 7b [613.4b], overwriting Duplicant's printed 2/4 with 4/4, and Duplicant's base power and toughness become those values [Duplicant ruling #0]. It also gains Zombie and Elemental and stays a Shapeshifter. Note that Duplicant's ability keeps updating: if the counters on the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card were somehow changed, Duplicant's power and toughness would change too [Duplicant ruling #3].

One nuance: Duplicant ruling #2 says abilities that add or subtract power/toughness (like Death's Shadow's) don't apply to the exiled card, only characteristic-defining abilities that define a *. That ruling is about abilities, not counters; the counters here are counters on the object itself, which set the card's power and toughness in exile per [122.1a].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the counters were already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when it was exiled. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had no counters at the moment of exile, Duplicant would simply be 1/1.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

gold_text.604.3a: Some static abilities are characteristic-defining abilities. A characteristic-defining ability conveys information about an object’s characteristics that would normally be found elsewhere on that object (such as in its mana cost, type line, or power/toughness box). Characteristic-defining abilities can add to or override information found elsewhere on that object. Characteristic-defining abilities function in all zones. A static ability is a characteristic-defining ability if it meets the following criteria: (1) It defines an object’s colors, subtypes, power, or toughness; (2) it is printed on the card it affects, it was granted to the token it affects by the effect that created the token, or it was acquired by the object it affects as the result of a copy effect or text-changing effect; (3) it does not directly affect the characteristics of any other objects; (4) it is not an ability that an object grants to itself; and (5) it does not set the values of such characteristics only if certain conditions are met.

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands taps only for white mana ({W}).

Why: both Magus of the Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Conversion ("All Mountains are Plains") are continuous type-changing effects applied in the same layer (CR 613 layer 4, type-changing). Normally timestamp order would apply Conversion first, but Conversion depends on Magus of the Moon: applying Magus of the Moon changes what Conversion applies to (which permanents are Mountains). Neither is a characteristic-defining ability, so the dependent effect (Conversion) is applied last.

Step by step:
1. Magus of the Moon applies: Badlands is a nonbasic land, so its subtypes become just Mountain. Per CR 305.7 it loses its old land types (Swamp, Mountain as printed) and the abilities generated from them, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6, Magus of the Moon ruling #4). It keeps its name Badlands and is still nonbasic (Magus of the Moon ruling #1).
2. Conversion then applies to Badlands because it is now a Mountain: its subtype becomes Plains, again stripping the Mountain type and the {R} mana ability and granting the intrinsic Plains ability "{T}: Add {W}" (CR 305.6, CR 305.7).

End result: Badlands is a nonbasic land with the single subtype Plains and only the mana ability "{T}: Add {W}" — no black, no red. Its printed "{T}: Add {B} or {R}" is gone because those abilities came from its old land types (Badlands ruling #3, Badlands ruling #1).

Timing note: this is a static continuous effect, so there is no window after Magus of the Moon resolves in which Badlands can still be tapped for {B} or {R} (Conversion ruling #0). If instead Alijah taps Badlands for {B} or {R} in response to the Magus of the Moon spell (before it resolves), that mana is produced normally.

Player count doesn't matter here — both effects are controlled by Alijah and apply the same way in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste).

Why: Both Fleetfeather Sandals' "Equipped creature has flying and haste" and Tightening Coils' "loses flying" are ability-adding/removing effects applied in layer 6, so they're ordered by timestamp, and the most recent one prevails (CR 113.10c, 613.1). Fleetfeather Sandals was attached first, so originally Tightening Coils' later timestamp won and Wandering Ones lost flying. But CR 613.7e says an Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object — and re-activating equip targeting the same creature still makes it become attached anew, so Fleetfeather Sandals (and the continuous effect from its static ability, CR 613.7a) now has a timestamp later than Tightening Coils. Applying layer 6 in order: Tightening Coils removes flying, then Fleetfeather Sandals grants flying and haste. Net result: Wandering Ones has flying and haste. This matches Tightening Coils ruling #0: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying.

Tightening Coils' -6/-0 is a layer 7c effect and is unaffected by the re-equip, so Wandering Ones is a -5/1 flier (power is treated as 0 for damage purposes; it doesn't die, since only 0-or-less toughness is lethal).

Note: only Adriel, as controller of Fleetfeather Sandals, can activate its equip ability (CR 301.5d), and equip only targets a creature Adriel controls — that's satisfied here. Nothing about this changes with more than two players; it's purely a timestamp/layers question between Adriel's and Nico's permanents.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger ends up as a colorless 2/2 artifact creature named Soldevi Digger, with no subtypes (no longer an Equipment) and no abilities at all — it loses both its own "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" and the equip ability Bludgeon Brawl was granting it.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1, 613.6, 110.3):

- Layer 4 (types/subtypes): Bludgeon Brawl only applies to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact." Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger an artifact creature. Because applying Titania's Song changes whether Bludgeon Brawl applies to Soldevi Digger at all, Titania's Song is applied first in layer 4 as a dependency; once Soldevi Digger is a creature, Bludgeon Brawl's ability simply doesn't apply to it anymore, so the Equipment subtype goes away. (Either way you order it, re-checking Bludgeon Brawl's condition against the live state gives the same result — Soldevi Digger is a creature, so no Equipment.) Note Titania's Song says "becomes an artifact creature," and per CR 205.1b such an effect lets the object keep its prior card types, so it's Artifact Creature, not just Creature.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Titania's Song's "loses all abilities" removes Soldevi Digger's activated ability. Even in a hypothetical where Bludgeon Brawl's grant were still applying (older timestamp), Titania's Song's later-timestamped removal would strip equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +X/+0" anyway.
- Layer 7b (P/T setting): Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to mana value. Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2} — two generic mana — so its mana value is 2, making it 2/2. This applies even though the definition of the effect refers to noncreature artifacts (CR 613.6).

Color is unchanged: nothing here changes color, and Soldevi Digger's mana cost has no colored symbols, so it stays colorless.

Also note the "leaves the battlefield" clause on Titania's Song: if Titania's Song leaves the battlefield, its effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays a 2/2 ability-less artifact creature (and thus still not an Equipment) for the rest of that turn.

None of this depends on player count — Bludgeon Brawl and Titania's Song affect artifacts regardless of controller, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities, controlled by Ariah.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1, 613.1g):

- Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes Wayward Angel a Frog creature, losing Angel and Horror.
- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's own threshold ability has the earlier timestamp and makes it black (Wayward Angel ruling #0: black, not white and black). Then Turn to Frog, with the later timestamp, sets its color to blue, overwriting that (CR 613.7). Final color: blue only.
- Layer 6 (abilities): the threshold ability applies first (timestamp order), granting trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature." Then Turn to Frog removes all abilities — flying, vigilance, the threshold ability itself, and everything threshold just granted. Final: no abilities. (Anything granted after Turn to Frog resolves would stick — Turn to Frog ruling #3.)
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 (CR 613.4b, 208.4a/208.4b, Turn to Frog ruling #0).
- Layer 7c (modifying P/T): here's the key point — even though the threshold ability was stripped in layer 6, CR 613.6 says an effect that has started to apply in one layer keeps applying in every other applicable layer. Threshold already started applying in layer 5, so its +3/+3 still applies in 7c: 1/1 becomes 4/4 (CR 613.4d for sublayer order).

This assumes Ariah still has seven or more cards in their graveyard when Turn to Frog resolves and afterward; the threshold effect only started applying because threshold was active. If the graveyard drops below seven cards later, the +3/+3 stops applying and Wayward Angel becomes a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities.

Nothing here depends on player count — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
After Ariella turns it face up, Wayward Angel is a 1/1 black Frog creature with no abilities (no flying, no vigilance, no trample, no upkeep sacrifice trigger).

Why:

1. While manifested, Wayward Angel was a 2/2 face-down colorless creature with no name, no subtypes, no abilities, and no mana cost — those are its copiable values while face down [701.40a, 708.2a]. Nathaniel's Turn to Frog resolving on it made it a blue Frog with base power/toughness 1/1 and no abilities.
2. Turning it face up is a special action Ariella can take any time she has priority, paying the card's mana cost {4}{W}{W} and showing all players it's a creature card [701.40b, 116.2b]. Turning it face up changes its copiable values back to those of Wayward Angel, but it does NOT end Turn to Frog — "any effects that have been applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent" [708.8, 708.10].
3. Now apply the layers to the restored copiable values (4/4 white Angel Horror with flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability) [613.1]:
   - Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog sets it to a Frog; it loses Angel and Horror but keeps the card type creature and any supertypes [Turn to Frog ruling #1].
   - Layer 5 (color): Turn to Frog (earlier timestamp) makes it blue; then Wayward Angel's own Threshold ability, with 7 cards in Ariella's graveyard, makes it black — and per the card's own text it is black, not white and black [Wayward Angel ruling #0]. Layer 5 is applied before layer 6, so the Threshold ability still exists to do this, exactly as in the Theros God example [Turn to Frog ruling #4].
   - Layer 6 (abilities): Turn to Frog removes all abilities, including flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability itself. From this layer onward the Threshold ability no longer exists, so it grants no trample and no upkeep sacrifice trigger.
   - Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base power/toughness to 1/1 [Turn to Frog ruling #0]. The Threshold +3/+3 in layer 7c doesn't apply because that ability was already removed in layer 6.
4. Nothing about turning it face up re-triggers enter-the-battlefield abilities [708.8, 701.40b].

Timing assumption: Turn to Frog resolved before Wayward Angel was turned face up, as stated. If instead Ariella had turned it face up first and Turn to Frog resolved afterward, the result would be the same set of characteristics here (1/1 blue Frog with no abilities) — except the color would be blue, since the later-timestamped Turn to Frog color effect would overwrite the Threshold black-setting effect in layer 5.

All of this is independent of player count; nothing here depends on there being exactly two players. If Ariella's graveyard drops below seven cards, the layer 5 Threshold color change stops applying and Wayward Angel would be blue.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret. Its full type line ends up: Legendary Land Creature — Swamp Ferret (a green 6/4).

How the layers get there (CR 613.1d, layer 4 for type changes; CR 613.6 for effects split across layers):

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth itself is a Swamp (Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0; CR 305.7 — gaining a land type in addition keeps existing types and rules text).
2. Kormus Bell then applies: "All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands." Because Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a Swamp, Kormus Bell makes it a land creature (CR 205.1b, 205.2b; Kormus Bell ruling #0). Kormus Bell's effect depends on Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's, since Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth changes what Kormus Bell applies to (CR 613.9).
3. Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land (Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5).
4. Conspiracy (naming Ferret) says creatures you control are the chosen type. Even though Conspiracy has the earliest timestamp, it's applied last in layer 4 here: whether Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature — i.e., whether Conspiracy applies to it at all — is determined by Kormus Bell and Vastwood Zendikon, so Conspiracy's effect depends on theirs (CR 613.9). Conspiracy sets the creature type, and affected creatures lose all their other creature types (Conspiracy ruling #4), so Elemental from Vastwood Zendikon is gone and Ferret is the only creature type. Conspiracy can also grant a creature type to animated lands that would otherwise have none (Conspiracy ruling #1).

What is unchanged: the Swamp subtype is a land type, not a creature type, so Conspiracy doesn't touch it; Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth keeps Swamp and the {T}: Add {B} ability that comes with it (CR 205.3c, 305.7). The Legendary supertype survives all of this (CR 205.4b). Colors and P/T are set in later layers by timestamp: layer 5 gives black (Kormus Bell) then green (Vastwood Zendikon), so it's green; layer 7b sets 1/1 then 6/4, so it's 6/4.

This analysis is player-count independent — nothing here depends on how many opponents are at the table; Conspiracy and Kormus Bell only care about creatures Ahmad controls and Swamps anywhere, respectively.

question: Andre controls [Raugrin Triome] and [Prismatic Omen]. Nala casts [Blood Moon]. After it resolves, what land types does Raugrin Triome have?
answer:
Raugrin Triome ends up with just one land type: Mountain.

Why: both effects apply in layer 4 (type-changing), and neither depends on the other, so they apply in timestamp order. Prismatic Omen (already on the battlefield) applies first, giving Raugrin Triome all five basic land types in addition to Island/Mountain/Plains [Prismatic Omen; Prismatic Omen ruling #0]. Blood Moon then resolves with a later timestamp and sets nonbasic lands' subtype to Mountain, which overwrites the earlier type-setting: per 305.7, when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses its old land types and the abilities generated from its rules text and old types, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6, Blood Moon ruling #2].

So after Blood Moon resolves, Raugrin Triome is a nonbasic land with the single subtype Mountain and the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" — no more {U} or {W}. Prismatic Omen doesn't rescue it: Prismatic Omen's older timestamp means its added types are wiped by Blood Moon, and Prismatic Omen never makes the land basic, so Blood Moon still applies to it [Prismatic Omen ruling #1, 205.4c, 305.8].

Notes: Blood Moon doesn't change names or supertypes, so the card is still named Raugrin Triome and is still nonbasic [Blood Moon ruling #1, 205.4b]. Its cycling {3} ability is a granted-from-rules-text ability of a land whose subtype was set, so it's gone too under 305.7 while Blood Moon applies. Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller.

If instead Blood Moon had been on the battlefield first and Prismatic Omen were cast afterward, Prismatic Omen's later timestamp would add all five basic types back on top of Mountain, and Raugrin Triome would tap for any color.

question: Ariel controls [Frostboil Snarl] and [Blood Moon]. They cast [Prismatic Omen]. After it resolves, what land types does Frostboil Snarl have?
answer:
Frostboil Snarl has all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.

Why: both effects apply in layer 4 (type-changing effects), in timestamp order (CR 613.1d).

1. Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") applies first. Frostboil Snarl is nonbasic (it has no "basic" supertype, CR 305.8/205.4c), so its land subtypes are set to just Mountain. Per CR 305.7 and 205.1a, setting a land's subtype to a basic land type wipes its old land types and the abilities from its rules text, replacing them with "{T}: Add {R}" ([Blood Moon ruling #2]). So its "As this land enters..." ability and "{T}: Add {U} or {R}" are gone.
2. Prismatic Omen then applies with the later timestamp. It adds every basic land type "in addition to their other types," so per CR 305.7's last sentence and CR 205.1b, Frostboil Snarl keeps Mountain and gains Plains, Island, Swamp, and Forest, plus the mana ability of each ([Prismatic Omen ruling #0]).

Net result: land types Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest; mana abilities "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {U}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", "{T}: Add {G}". Its name is still Frostboil Snarl, and it is still a nonbasic land — neither effect changes names or supertypes ([Blood Moon ruling #1], [Prismatic Omen ruling #1], CR 205.4b, CR 305.8). Because it remains nonbasic, Blood Moon keeps applying to it; the two effects coexist rather than one shutting off the other.

Assumption on timing: Frostboil Snarl and Blood Moon were already on the battlefield and Prismatic Omen resolved afterward. If instead Blood Moon had entered after Prismatic Omen, Blood Moon would have the later timestamp and would set Frostboil Snarl's subtypes to Mountain only (Prismatic Omen's earlier addition would be overwritten in layer 4).

Player count doesn't matter here: both enchantments are Ariel's own permanents, and Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of how many opponents are at the table.

question: Adan restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. Adan puts [Blood Moon], [Prismatic Omen] and [Winged Temple of Orazca] onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated. What colors of mana can Winged Temple of Orazca tap for?
answer:
Direct answer: Winged Temple of Orazca can no longer tap for "any color" via its own printed ability — that ability is gone. What it can tap for depends on the relative timestamps of the two type-changing effects, and in the ordering Adan would normally get (Blood Moon's type-setting applied first, Prismatic Omen's type-adding second) it taps for any of the five colors: {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}.

Why:

1. Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Winged Temple of Orazca is a nonbasic land, so per [305.7] and [Blood Moon ruling #2] its subtype is set to Mountain, it loses all abilities generated from its rules text (both "{T}: Add one mana of any color" and the {1}{G}{U}, {T} pump ability), and it gains the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" ([305.6], [Mountain]). Setting the subtype does not remove its Legendary supertype or its land card type ([305.7]).

2. Prismatic Omen says "Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types." Adding land types leaves rules text intact and grants the mana ability of each added basic land type ([305.7], [Prismatic Omen ruling #0]), i.e. {T}: Add {W} / {U} / {B} / {R} / {G} ([305.6], [Plains], [Mountain]).

3. Layer bookkeeping (both are type-changing effects in layer 4): neither effect changes what the other does or what it applies to, so there is no dependency — they apply in timestamp order. With Blood Moon first, the result is subtypes Mountain, Plains, Island, Swamp, Forest, no rules-text abilities, and therefore the five basic-land mana abilities: {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}. With Prismatic Omen's effect first, Blood Moon then wipes the subtypes back to just Mountain and the land taps only for {R}.

Timing assumption: Karn Liberated's −14 puts all the exiled cards onto the battlefield at once, so Blood Moon and Prismatic Omen enter simultaneously. The provided rules don't include the tie-breaking rule for timestamps of simultaneously-entering permanents, so I'm flagging that explicitly: under the ordering where Blood Moon's effect is the earlier timestamp you get all five colors; under the reverse you get only {R}. Either way, the "{T}: Add one mana of any color" and "{1}{G}{U}, {T}: Target creature you control gains flying and gets +X/+X" abilities printed on Winged Temple of Orazca are lost, since Blood Moon's card text overrides its printed rules text.

Note also that the mana it makes is ordinary colored mana; nothing here restricts how it can be spent ([106.6]). Player count doesn't matter — Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands and Prismatic Omen only Adan's lands, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a **Land Creature — Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest Island**, a 1/1 that's both blue and green.

How it gets there (all in layer 4, type-changing effects, CR 613.1d):

1. **Arcane Adaptation** (naming Saproling) makes Realmwright a Saproling in addition to its other types — it's now a Vedalken Wizard Saproling (CR 205.1b).
2. **Life and Limb** then applies, because Realmwright is now a Saproling: it becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature and a Forest land in addition to its other types. This is a dependency, not just timestamps — applying Arcane Adaptation changes what Life and Limb applies to, so Life and Limb is applied after it (CR 613.8, 613.8a). Realmwright now has card types Creature and Land, with Forest correlated to Land and Saproling/Vedalken/Wizard correlated to Creature (CR 205.3c, Life and Limb ruling #3).
3. **Realmwright's own** "Lands you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types" now applies, even though Realmwright entered first: Life and Limb changing Realmwright into a land changes what Realmwright's effect applies to, so Realmwright's effect depends on Life and Limb and is applied last (CR 613.8, 613.8a). It gains the land type Island as well.

Other consequences: because it gained the land types Forest and Island in addition to its own types, it keeps its rules text and gains the mana abilities of both — "{T}: Add {G}" and "{T}: Add {U}" (CR 305.7). Its color is blue (printed) plus green from Life and Limb's layer‑5 effect, and Life and Limb sets its power/toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b. It has no supertypes; nothing here grants or removes any (CR 205.4b). Being a land creature, it's subject to summoning sickness for tapping.

Note the order they entered doesn't ultimately matter here, since dependency overrides timestamps (CR 613.7, 613.8). This analysis is about Apollo's own permanents only, so it reads the same in a two-player or multiplayer game — each "you control" effect only affects Apollo's permanents.

question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes. The token will be legendary, and Ainsley will then have to put one of the two Awoken Demons into the graveyard.

Why: Helm of the Host's ability creates a token copy of the equipped creature "except the token isn't legendary." That exception is part of the copy effect, so the token's copiable values do not include the legendary supertype ([Helm of the Host ruling #3], [707.9f]). But Leyline of Singularity isn't a copy effect 	o on on top of the finished object: it says "All nonland permanents are legendary," a continuous effect that grants the supertype to every nonland permanent on the battlefield, including the newly created token. Adding a supertype doesn't remove any others ([205.4b], [Leyline of Singularity ruling #0]). So the token enters with Awoken Demon's copiable characteristics minus legendary, and Leyline of Singularity immediately makes it legendary anyway.

Consequence: "Legendary" is a supertype that subjects a permanent to the legend rule ([205.4d], [Legendary]). Because both the original Awoken Demon and the token are named Awoken Demon (a token copy takes the copied permanent's name, [111.4]) and both are legendary and controlled by Ainsley, the legend rule state-based action applies: Ainsley chooses one to keep and the other is put into its owner's graveyard ([704.5j], [Leyline of Singularity ruling #2]). The token does get haste, but that rarely helps since it may be the one sacrificed to the legend rule.

Timing note: I'm assuming Leyline of Singularity is already on the battlefield when the Helm of the Host trigger resolves, as stated. If Leyline of Singularity weren't there (or left before state-based actions were checked), the token would be nonlegendary and both Awoken Demons could coexist, per [Helm of the Host ruling #3].

Multiplayer: the legend rule only looks at permanents controlled by the same player, so the answer is identical whether the game has two players or more; opponents' Awoken Demons are irrelevant ([704.5j]).

question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
answer:
Direct answer: the two basic lands (Snow-Covered Island and Mountain) end up with all five basic land types and all five mana abilities; the two nonbasic lands (Study Hall and Dryad Arbor) end up as plain Mountains with only "{T}: Add {R}."

Why: Dryad of the Ilysian Grove has the older timestamp and adds land types ("in addition to their other types"), so in layer 4 every land Addison controls gains Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest, keeping its own types and rules text [305.7, 613.6, Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0]. Blood Moon then applies with the later timestamp and *sets* the subtypes of nonbasic lands to Mountain, which wipes out the earlier-granted land types and every ability from rules text or old land types [305.7, Blood Moon ruling #2]. Neither effect changes what the other applies to (Blood Moon keys off the "basic" supertype, which nothing here changes), so there's no dependency and plain timestamp order governs [205.4b, 205.4c, Blood Moon ruling #1].

Results:
- Snow-Covered Island — Basic Snow Land — Island Plains Swamp Mountain Forest. Basic (supertype "basic"), so Blood Moon ignores it [205.4c]. It has {T}: Add {U}, {T}: Add {W}, {T}: Add {B}, {T}: Add {R}, and {T}: Add {G} [305.6]. Snow is still a supertype [205.4b, Snow-Covered Island ruling #0].
- Mountain — Basic Land — Mountain Plains Island Swamp Forest, likewise unaffected by Blood Moon, with all five basic mana abilities [305.6, 205.4c].
- Study Hall — Land — Mountain. Nonbasic, so Blood Moon sets its type to Mountain and it loses "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color" ability; its only ability is "{T}: Add {R}" [305.7, 305.6, Blood Moon ruling #2]. Note {C} (colorless) is gone entirely — {R} is not a substitute for it.
- Dryad Arbor — Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, still green, still 1/1. Setting land subtypes doesn't touch card types, creature types, or its color indicator [305.7, 205.3c, Dryad Arbor ruling #0, Dryad Arbor ruling #2, Dryad Arbor ruling #3]. Its mana ability is now "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}", and it's still subject to summoning sickness for tapping.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dryad of the Ilysian Grove was already on the battlefield when Blood Moon resolved (as stated). If instead Blood Moon were already out and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entered later, Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's effect would have the later timestamp and would add all five basic types back on top of Blood Moon's Mountain, giving every land Addison controls all five basic mana abilities (nonbasic lands still would not get their original printed abilities back, since Blood Moon keeps stripping those).

Player count doesn't matter here: Dryad of the Ilysian Grove only affects lands Addison controls, and Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller, so in a multiplayer game opponents' nonbasic lands are also Mountains with just "{T}: Add {R}," but they get no extra basic land types.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Nico's Thespian's Stage is hit by Alpine Moon; Alayna's own Thespian's Stage is not.

Nico's permanent (Thespian's Stage copying Temple of Triumph): its copiable values are those of Temple of Triumph, including its name, plus the granted "{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" (707.3, 707.9b; Thespian's Stage ruling #0 — it no longer has the Stage's mana ability "{T}: Add {C}"). Because its name is now literally "Temple of Triumph" — the chosen name — and Nico is an opponent of Alayna, Alpine Moon applies. Applying the layers (613.1c): in layer 4 it loses all land types (Temple of Triumph has none printed anyway, so no visible change), and in layer 6 it loses all abilities — including the "enters tapped" and "scry 1" abilities, the {R}/{W} mana ability, and the copy ability it kept as an exception — and then gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Result: a land named Temple of Triumph with no land types and exactly one ability, "{T}: Add one mana of any color." It keeps the land card type and any supertypes (Alpine Moon ruling #1), and it stays tapped or untapped as it already was (Thespian's Stage ruling #2). Notably it can no longer activate the copy ability, since Alpine Moon strips it.

Alayna's second Thespian's Stage: it copies Temple of Triumph (whether it targeted a real one or Nico's permanent — the copiable values are the same, and if it targeted Nico's permanent the Alpine Moon effect is not copied, since only copiable values are copied per 707.3). So it becomes a land named Temple of Triumph with "{T}: Add {R} or {W}", the enters-tapped and scry abilities (which do nothing now — it was already on the battlefield, per Thespian's Stage ruling #1), plus "{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability." Alpine Moon only affects lands Alayna's *opponents* control, and Alayna controls this one, so it is untouched, and it doesn't become untapped from copying (Thespian's Stage ruling #2).

Multiplayer note: Alpine Moon says "lands your opponents control," so at a table of more than two players every opponent's land named Temple of Triumph — including copies like Nico's — is affected the same way; Alayna's own are always exempt.

Timing assumption: Alpine Moon's name choice was made as it entered and Nico's Stage was already a copy of Temple of Triumph. If Nico instead copies Temple of Triumph *after* Alpine Moon is on the battlefield, the answer is the same — Alpine Moon is a continuous effect that applies to whatever qualifying lands exist at any moment.

question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
One with the Stars wins on card type: Thraben Purebloods ends up as a noncreature enchantment — a green enchantment with no abilities and no creature types.

Step by step, by layer (rule 613.6 splits each Aura's effect into the layers it belongs to):

- Layer 4 (types): Kenrith's Transformation makes Thraben Purebloods an Elk creature that loses its other card types and creature types. One with the Stars has the later timestamp, so it's applied second in that same layer (613.7): Thraben Purebloods becomes an enchantment and loses all other card types, including the creature type it had from Kenrith's Transformation. Per One with the Stars ruling #2, it also loses the subtypes tied to the lost card types, so the Elk creature type goes away. Supertypes would be kept (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3, One with the Stars ruling #2), though Thraben Purebloods has none.
- Layer 5 (color): Kenrith's Transformation still makes Thraben Purebloods green; One with the Stars doesn't touch color.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Kenrith's Transformation removes all of Thraben Purebloods's abilities. One with the Stars's reminder text "It still has its abilities" doesn't hand any back — it isn't granting abilities, it just isn't removing any (113.12). So Thraben Purebloods has no abilities. Anything that grants it an ability later would stick (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #6).
- Layer 7b (P/T): Kenrith's Transformation still sets base power/toughness 3/3, but since Thraben Purebloods isn't a creature, that value is irrelevant while One with the Stars is attached.

Note both Auras remain legally attached: Kenrith's Transformation has "enchant creature," but enchant is only checked on targeting/attachment and by state-based actions for legality — that's not in the provided rules here, so treat this as the practical result the two cards' own text produces. One with the Stars ruling #1 confirms its effect keeps the permanent an enchantment even after a temporary creature-making effect ends.

If One with the Stars later leaves the battlefield, only Kenrith's Transformation's layer-4 effect remains, and Thraben Purebloods goes back to being a green 3/3 Elk creature with no abilities.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
Result: a face-down mutated permanent that is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types other than creature (no subtypes), no mana cost — the characteristics granted by its face-down status — but it also has Trumpeting Gnarr's triggered ability, and Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate trigger does trigger, so Avery creates a 3/3 green Beast creature token.

Why:
- Trumpeting Gnarr cast for its mutate cost doesn't enter the battlefield; it merges with the target creature and the two cards become one object, a mutated permanent [702.140c], [608.3d], [730.1]. Avery chose the manifested card on top, so Trumpeting Gnarr is the bottom component.
- The merged permanent's characteristics come from the topmost component, while it has the abilities of every component [702.140e], [Mutating Creature Spell]. Topmost here is the manifested card, which is face down, so the permanent is a nameless, colorless 2/2 creature; the abilities of Trumpeting Gnarr (its mutate trigger) still apply because abilities come from all components.
- Status (face up/face down is one of the four status categories, alongside tapped/untapped, flipped/unflipped, phased in/out) [110.5] is set by the topmost component of a merged permanent, so the whole permanent is face down [730.2e]. Note the sentence in 730.2e that other effects don't count a face-down permanent as being "turned face up" if merging makes it face up — that's the reverse case and doesn't apply here.
- These merge-based characteristic changes are applied in layer 1a, the copiable-effects sublayer, in timestamp order [613.2a], [613.7].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Soul Summons fully resolved (the card is already a face-down 2/2 on the battlefield) before Trumpeting Gnarr was cast targeting it; the mutate target must be a creature already on the battlefield, and a face-down creature has no creature types, so it isn't a Human and is a legal target.

One caveat the provided rules don't settle: they don't spell out what happens if Avery later turns the manifested card face up while it's part of this merged permanent (730.2j only covers merged permanents containing double-faced components). Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
answer:
Yes — Mist Dragon still has flying (and is an 8/8 until end of turn).

Why: after the two Spontaneous Flights, Mist Dragon has two flying counters, and Hex Parasite removes only one of them, so one flying counter is still there. Counters are identical and interchangeable, so what remains is simply "a flying counter on Mist Dragon," which grants flying.

Walking the timeline in layer 6 (ability adding/removing), applied in timestamp order (CR 613.1, 613.7a, 113.10c):
1. First Spontaneous Flight resolves: +2/+2 until end of turn and a flying counter — Mist Dragon has flying.
2. April activates Mist Dragon's "{0}: This creature loses flying." That's a later effect that removes all instances of flying (CR 113.10b), so at that moment Mist Dragon has no flying. (Note this is an indefinite effect, not a one-shot.)
3. Second Spontaneous Flight resolves: another +2/+2 and a second flying counter. That counter's grant is more recent than the lose-flying effect, so the most recent effect prevails and Mist Dragon has flying again (CR 113.10c, 613.9).
4. Hex Parasite removes one flying counter (and gets +1/+0). One flying counter remains, still later in timestamp than the lose-flying activation, so Mist Dragon keeps flying. Extra instances of flying would have been redundant anyway (CR 702.9c).

Power/toughness: 4/4 base, +2/+2 twice from the two Spontaneous Flights = 8/8 until end of turn.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming exactly the order you gave, with each spell/ability fully resolving before the next. If instead April had activated "loses flying" *after* Hex Parasite's activation resolved, that lose-flying effect would be the most recent layer-6 effect and Mist Dragon would not have flying — April can always re-activate "{0}: This creature loses flying" or "{0}: This creature gains flying" to change the answer, since the latest activation wins.

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the result is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game (Hex Parasite could be controlled by any player and the outcome is unchanged).

question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
answer:
Fiend Artisan is -1/1 (power -1, toughness 1) while enchanted by Mystic Subdual.

Why: continuous effects apply in layers (CR 613.1). Fiend Artisan's printed power/toughness is 1/1 (CR 302.4c). Its ability "This creature gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard" is not a characteristic-defining ability that sets base power/toughness — it's a modifying effect applied in layer 7c (CR 613.4c). Mystic Subdual's "loses all abilities" applies earlier, in layer 6, so by the time we reach layer 7c, Fiend Artisan no longer has that ability and it never starts applying (CR 613.6 only preserves an effect that had already begun applying in an earlier layer). So the +4/+4 from the four creature cards in Aimee's graveyard is simply gone.

Mystic Subdual's own -2/-0 is a separate part of the same ability and does apply in layer 7c, giving 1/1 → -1/1. A creature's power can be negative; its toughness of 1 means it isn't destroyed by state-based actions on its own.

Note Mystic Subdual ruling #1 covers the related but different case of a */* creature whose ability defines its power and toughness: there the base becomes 0/0 and the Aura makes it -2/0. Fiend Artisan is printed 1/1, not */*, so it keeps base 1/1 and ends at -1/1.

Ordering/timing: this is the state as long as Mystic Subdual remains attached; the layer result doesn't depend on the order the two were put onto the battlefield, since layer 6 always precedes layer 7. If Mystic Subdual leaves the battlefield, Fiend Artisan immediately regains its ability and becomes 5/5 with four creature cards in Aimee's graveyard. Also, per Fiend Artisan ruling #0, any damage already marked on it stays marked, so damage that was nonlethal at 5/5 can become lethal at toughness 1. Nothing here changes with more than two players — the count is of creature cards in your (Fiend Artisan's controller's, i.e. Aimee's) graveyard only.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
answer:
The mutated creature will be 1/1 with no abilities, and it gets no +1/+1 counters.

Why:

1. Mutate merges the two cards into one permanent. With Glowstone Recluse on top, the resulting mutated permanent's non-ability characteristics (name, types, colors, printed power/toughness 2/3) come from Glowstone Recluse, and it would have the abilities of both cards ([702.140c], [702.140e], [Mutating Creature Spell]). That merge is a layer 1a copiable change ([613.2a]), so the permanent's starting P/T is 2/3.

2. Humility's effect applies in two layers ([613.1], [Humility ruling #2]): layer 6 — the creature loses all abilities (so Reach and "Whenever this creature mutates..." are gone); layer 7b — its base power and toughness are set to 1/1 ([613.4b], [Base Power, Base Toughness]).

3. Result: 1/1, no abilities.

4. The mutate trigger never happens. "Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it" triggers when the spell merges with the creature ([702.140d]), but at that moment the permanent already has no abilities because of Humility (layer 6), so there is no ability there to trigger. No counters are created, and therefore nothing to add in layer 7c on top of the 1/1 ([302.4c]).

Timing notes/assumptions: I'm assuming Humility is already on the battlefield and stays there through the mutate spell's resolution. If Humility had entered after the mutate resolved, the counters would already have been placed and would still apply in layer 7c (counters modify P/T and aren't removed by Humility), making the creature 3/3 — Humility only sets base P/T in 7b. Also, if Maritime Guard were somehow an illegal target on resolution, Glowstone Recluse would just enter the battlefield as its own creature ([702.140b]) and would likewise be 1/1 under Humility.

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
answer:
Forgotten Monument is still a land, but it is now a Mountain: its type line is effectively "Land — Mountain," it's colorless, it has no supertypes, it has lost both of its printed abilities ({T}: Add {C} and the Cave-granting ability), and its only ability is the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}." It remains under Alex's control and is not a creature.

Why: Lizard, Connors's Curse's trigger makes Magus of the Moon lose all abilities (layer 6) and become a green Lizard with base 4/4 (layers 4, 5, 7b), and that effect doesn't end at end of turn [Lizard, Connors's Curse ruling #0]. But Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-changing effect applied in layer 4, which is applied before the layer-6 ability-removal effect, regardless of the order the effects began [613.6], [Magus of the Moon ruling #0]. So Magus of the Moon keeps Mountain-ing nonbasic lands even after it has no abilities.

Setting a nonbasic land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose its old land types (Cave), all abilities from its rules text, and any copiable effects on it, and gain the mana ability for the new basic land type [305.7], [305.6], [Magus of the Moon ruling #4]. Magus of the Moon does not change card types or supertypes and does not change the name, so Forgotten Monument is still named Forgotten Monument and is still a land — not a basic land [305.7], [205.4b], [Magus of the Moon ruling #1].

Side effect: because Forgotten Monument is no longer a Cave and no longer has its granting ability, any other Caves Alex controls lose the "{T}, Pay 1 life: Add one mana of any color" ability (and any other nonbasic Caves are themselves Mountains anyway).

This answer is the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller, so every player's nonbasic lands are Mountains too.
