question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?
answer:
Yes — Skeletal Snake has flying, and it's a 12/11.

Why: Rune of Flight is an Aura enchanting the Equipment Colossus Hammer, so its third ability doesn't apply (Colossus Hammer isn't a creature), but its fourth does: it grants Colossus Hammer the ability "Equipped creature has flying." Now Colossus Hammer has two relevant abilities affecting the equipped creature — its own "Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying" and the granted "Equipped creature has flying."

Both of these are ability-adding/removing effects that apply in layer 6, so order is by timestamp [613.7a]. A continuous effect from a static ability takes the timestamp of the object it's on or of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later — the granted ability's timestamp comes from Rune of Flight, which is later than Colossus Hammer's own. When Colossus Hammer then becomes attached to Skeletal Snake it receives a new timestamp [613.7e], and both of its abilities get new timestamps too, but their relative order is preserved [613.7a]. So Colossus Hammer's own "loses flying" applies first, then the Rune-granted "has flying" applies after it — Skeletal Snake ends up with flying. This matches the ruling that a creature gaining flying after Colossus Hammer is attached keeps flying [Colossus Hammer ruling #2]. Separately, in layer 7c the +10/+10 makes the 2/1 Skeletal Snake a 12/11.

Note that "loses flying" isn't a one-shot event; it's a continuous effect, which is why layer/timestamp order decides this rather than "whichever happened last in play." Also note Skeletal Snake had no flying to begin with — that's fine, Colossus Hammer can equip a creature without flying [Colossus Hammer ruling #0].

One caution on ordering: this answer assumes Rune of Flight was attached to Colossus Hammer *before* Colossus Hammer was equipped, as stated. If instead Colossus Hammer were already attached to Skeletal Snake and Rune of Flight came down afterward, the answer is the same — Rune of Flight's grant would still have the later timestamp and Skeletal Snake would still have flying. The Snake only lacks flying if some effect gives Colossus Hammer's own ability a later timestamp than the granted one (e.g. re-equipping doesn't do this, since relative order is preserved).

Player count doesn't matter here; none of these rules depend on the number of players. Note also that Colossus Hammer's controller and Skeletal Snake's controller could differ [301.5d], but here Ainsley controls both.

question: Ashley equips [Colossus Hammer] to [Ogre Warrior], then enchants it with [Phantom Wings]. Does Ogre Warrior have flying?
answer:
Yes — Ogre Warrior has flying, and it's a 13/13.

Both Colossus Hammer's "loses flying" and Phantom Wings' "Enchanted creature has flying" are ability-adding/removing continuous effects applied in layer 6, and neither depends on the other, so they're applied in timestamp order and the later one wins [613.9], [613.7a]. Colossus Hammer was attached first, so its effect has the earlier timestamp; Phantom Wings, attached second, has the later timestamp and grants flying afterward [613.7e]. This matches the Colossus Hammer ruling that a creature which gains flying after Colossus Hammer became attached keeps flying [Colossus Hammer ruling #2].

Separately, in layer 7c Colossus Hammer still gives +10/+10, so Ogre Warrior (base 3/3) is a 13/13 with flying.

Timing caveat: this assumes the order stated in the question (Hammer first, then the Aura). If instead Phantom Wings had been attached first and Colossus Hammer equipped afterward, Colossus Hammer's effect would have the later timestamp and Ogre Warrior would be a 13/13 without flying. Note also that if Colossus Hammer later becomes attached again, it receives a new timestamp and could then win [613.7e].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the result is the same in two-player and multiplayer games. (Ogre Warrior is also "modified" while equipped and enchanted by an Aura Ashley controls [700.9], though no card here cares about that.)

question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?
answer:
Yes. Ari's Dormant Volcano is a Mountain (and nothing else in the way of land types), with the ability "{T}: Add {R}" replacing its "{T}: Add {C}{R}" and its other abilities.

Why: Ichthyomorphosis makes the enchanted Magus of the Moon lose all abilities and be a blue Fish with base power/toughness 0/1. But the type-changing effect from Magus of the Moon's ability ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") is applied in layer 4, while ability-removal is applied in layer 6, so the subtype change is locked in before the abilities are stripped — regardless of which effect started first [613.1d], [613.6]. This is stated directly by the ruling: if Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it still turns nonbasic lands into Mountains [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].

Consequences for Dormant Volcano: setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose its old land types, its rules-text abilities, and any copiable effects on it, and it gains the mana ability for the new type [305.7], [Magus of the Moon ruling #4]. So Dormant Volcano loses "This land enters tapped," its enters-the-battlefield sacrifice trigger, and "{T}: Add {C}{R}," and instead has "{T}: Add {R}" — note it no longer produces the colorless {C}, only the red {R}.

It is not a basic land: Magus of the Moon doesn't touch supertypes or names, so Dormant Volcano is a nonbasic land whose land type is Mountain, still named Dormant Volcano [Magus of the Moon ruling #1], [205.4b], [305.7].

One check: Ichthyomorphosis stays attached only while Magus of the Moon is still a creature; Ichthyomorphosis itself makes it a Fish creature, so it remains legally enchanted [Ichthyomorphosis ruling #5]. Timing note: it doesn't matter whether Ichthyomorphosis was attached before or after Magus of the Moon entered — layers, not timestamps, decide this [613.6].

Multiplayer: no difference. Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so every player's nonbasic lands become Mountains at any table size.

question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up a black 6/6 Angel Horror creature with no abilities.

Step by step through the layers (CR 613.1), with Wayward Angel's threshold ability having an earlier timestamp than Humility:

- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's threshold ability is active (7+ cards in Averie's graveyard), so Wayward Angel is black — and only black, not white and black (Wayward Angel ruling #0).
- Layer 6 (abilities): First, at timestamp order, Wayward Angel's own threshold ability grants it trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature." Then Humility, with the later timestamp, removes all abilities from all creatures — including Wayward Angel's flying, vigilance, the threshold ability itself, and the trample/upkeep ability it just granted. Wayward Angel now has no abilities.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modifications): Muraganda Petroglyphs checks the live state — Wayward Angel genuinely has no abilities at this point, and Humility's "loses all abilities" is an effect removing abilities, not something that leaves an ability behind (CR 113.12), so Wayward Angel gets +2/+2 → 3/3. Then Wayward Angel's threshold effect still applies +3/+3, because per CR 613.6 an effect that started applying in an earlier layer (layer 5, where it made Wayward Angel black) continues to apply in every later applicable layer even though the ability generating it was removed in layer 6. That's the same principle spelled out in Humility ruling #2. Result: 6/6.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Humility resolved after Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield (as stated), giving Humility the later timestamp. If instead Wayward Angel entered after Humility, layer 6 would go the other way — Humility strips abilities first, then Wayward Angel's threshold grant would re-add trample and the upkeep ability, so Wayward Angel would have those abilities, Muraganda Petroglyphs would not apply, and it would be a black 4/4 with trample and the sacrifice trigger. (Note that the threshold ability would still be functioning to grant them, since Humility's removal already applied.)

Player count doesn't matter here: Humility affects all creatures and Muraganda Petroglyphs affects all creatures with no abilities regardless of controller, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Urza's Saga is put into Nico's graveyard as a state-based action almost immediately after Jinx resolves.

Why:

1. Jinx says "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn." That's a type-changing effect applied in layer 4 ([613.1d], [Type-Changing Effect]). Setting a land's subtype replaces its existing land types, so Urza's Saga loses the Urza's land type and gains the chosen basic land type plus that type's intrinsic mana ability, and it loses all abilities generated from its rules text ([305.7], [205.1a]).
2. Setting a land subtype does not change card types or supertypes ([305.7], [205.4b]). Urza's Saga is still an Enchantment Land, and "Saga" is an enchantment subtype, not a land subtype — Jinx only replaces subtypes from the land-type set ([205.1a]). So Urza's Saga is still a Saga, but with no chapter abilities.
3. A Saga with no chapter abilities is sacrificed immediately — this is exactly the situation covered by [Urza's Saga ruling #1] ("If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed"). Having two lore counters doesn't protect it. See also [Urza's Saga ruling #4], confirming it remains a Saga even though it's a land.

A note on abilities it had already gained: chapter I's "{T}: Add {C}" (and chapter II's token ability if it had resolved) were granted by a separate effect, and [305.7] says setting a land's subtype doesn't remove abilities granted to the land by other effects; [Urza's Saga ruling #5] says it keeps those for as long as it's on the battlefield. But since it's sacrificed right away, that matters only if Nico can respond — Jinx's target change happens on resolution, so Nico can tap Urza's Saga for {C} (colorless mana specifically, not generic) or activate the Construct-token ability in response to Jinx while it's still on the stack.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming chapter II has already resolved (two lore counters) and Jinx resolves before Nico's next draw step. If instead a third lore counter were added first, chapter III would trigger and Urza's Saga would be sacrificed after that chapter resolves ([Urza's Saga ruling #4]) — Jinx afterward would find nothing.

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of players; the result is the same whether it's a two-player game or a larger table.

question: Aaden activates [Inkmoth Nexus], equips [Colossus Hammer] to it, then activates Inkmoth Nexus again. What are the characteristics of Inkmoth Nexus?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus ends up as an 11/11 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with flying and infect, equipped with Colossus Hammer.

How the layers get there (CR 613.6, 613.7):

- Layer 4 (types): both activations of Inkmoth Nexus make it an artifact creature Phyrexian Blinkmoth that's still a land; per CR 205.1b, "It's still a land" means it keeps the land type (and any supertypes, CR 205.4b). Net: Artifact Land Creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth.
- Layer 5 (color): nothing changes its color, so Inkmoth Nexus stays colorless.
- Layer 6 (abilities), in timestamp order: first activation grants flying and infect; then Colossus Hammer's "equipped creature ... loses flying" removes flying; then the second activation of Inkmoth Nexus (latest timestamp) grants flying and infect again. So flying is back, and infect is there.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): both activations set it to 1/1; the later one (second activation) wins, so base 1/1.
- Layer 7c (modifying P/T): Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 applies, giving 11/11.

Note that Colossus Hammer's ability keeps applying in layer 7c even though a later effect re-granted flying — the Hammer is still attached and its P/T part is unaffected; only the flying-removal was overwritten by the later ability-granting effect (CR 613.6, 613.7). Colossus Hammer legally stays attached because Inkmoth Nexus is still a creature (CR 301.5c). If Inkmoth Nexus stopped being a creature (e.g., at end of turn), Colossus Hammer would become unattached as a state-based action (CR 301.5c, 704.1), and Inkmoth Nexus would have no power or toughness at all as a noncreature permanent (CR 208.3a).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the order given — activate, then equip, then activate again. If the second activation had come before equipping Colossus Hammer, the Hammer's flying-removal would have the latest timestamp and Inkmoth Nexus would be an 11/11 artifact creature land with infect but no flying.

None of this depends on player count; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Ari casts [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze], with two spells having been cast before then. Nadia controls [Humility]. What will Ari's battlefield look like once the stack fully resolves and state-based actions are checked?
answer:
Ari ends up with three green Ooze creatures, all with no abilities: two nonlegendary Aeve, Progenitor Ooze tokens (a 1/1 and a 2/2) and the real, legendary Aeve, Progenitor Ooze card as a 3/3. Nothing dies and the legend rule doesn't apply.

How that shakes out:

1. Storm copies. Two spells were cast before Aeve, Progenitor Ooze this turn, so storm copies it twice; per Aeve, Progenitor Ooze's own reminder text those copies become tokens (a copy of a spell/ability is itself a spell or ability, CR 707.10e). Per [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2] the two storm copies resolve and enter the battlefield one at a time, then the original spell resolves last.

2. Counters as they enter. "Aeve enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each other Ooze you control" is a replacement effect that applies as the permanent enters (CR 614.1), while it is not yet on the battlefield, so Humility (which affects creatures on the battlefield) does not stop the counters. Assuming Ari controlled no other Oozes beforehand: first token enters with 0 counters, second token with 1 counter, and the original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze with 2 counters ([Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2]).

3. Layers (CR 613 ordering, checked with the layer resolver). Humility has the earlier timestamp; each Aeve, Progenitor Ooze permanent enters later.
   - Layer 4: each token's own "Aeve isn't legendary if it's a token" applies before Humility's ability-removal in layer 6, and per the Humility rulings on layer interaction ([Humility ruling #2]) an effect that has started applying keeps applying even after the ability is stripped — so the two tokens are nonlegendary.
   - Layer 6: Humility removes all abilities from all three (storm, the non-legendary clause's source, and the counters ability are all gone from the objects going forward).
   - Layer 7b: Humility sets base power/toughness 1/1.
   - Layer 7c: +1/+1 counters still apply on top — they are physical counters, not abilities. Token A: 1/1. Token B: 2/2. Original: 3/3.

4. State-based actions: none of them are 0 toughness, and since both tokens are nonlegendary, the legend rule never triggers against the legendary nontoken Aeve, Progenitor Ooze. All three stay.

Timing note: if Ari already controlled other Oozes before casting, add one counter (and +1/+1) to each of the three for every such Ooze on the battlefield at that moment.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players — Humility is Nadia's but affects all creatures regardless of controller, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?
answer:
One with the Stars can't be cast targeting Capenna Express at that moment, so the crew ability resolves normally and Capenna Express becomes a 6/6 artifact creature until end of turn.

Why: One with the Stars says "Enchant creature or enchantment." At the time Natalie would cast it, Allen has only activated Capenna Express's crew ability — that ability is still on the stack and hasn't resolved, so Capenna Express is still just an artifact Vehicle with no creature or enchantment type. Crew N means "Tap any number of other untapped creatures you control with total power N or greater: This permanent becomes an artifact creature until end of turn" [702.122a], and that type change only happens on resolution. A Vehicle is a noncreature permanent until then and doesn't even have power or toughness [208.3a, 301.7]. Because Capenna Express isn't a legal object for One with the Stars's enchant ability, Natalie can't choose it as a target when casting; the spell simply can't be cast that way (High Fae Trickster's "You may cast spells as though they had flash" fixes the timing, not the legality of the target).

What Natalie should do instead: let the crew ability resolve. Once Capenna Express is an artifact creature, it's a legal target, and she can then cast One with the Stars with flash granted by High Fae Trickster. On resolution Capenna Express becomes an enchantment and loses all other card types — and per the ruling, it stays an enchantment even after the "until end of turn" crew effect would have worn off [One with the Stars ruling #1]. It keeps its abilities but is no longer an artifact, a Vehicle, or a creature, so it can't attack.

Timing caveat: if instead Capenna Express had already been animated before Natalie cast (for example, Allen had already sacrificed a Treasure with its other ability), then One with the Stars would have a legal target and would resolve, stripping the creature and artifact types; the later-resolving crew ability would then apply its own "becomes an artifact creature until end of turn" effect on top of that. The layer/timestamp rules governing which of those two type-changing effects ends up on top weren't included in the context, so I can't state that outcome definitively.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it works the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Aitana casts [Finale of Devastation] with X = 10. Will the creature they find have haste?
answer:
Yes — the creature Aitana finds will have haste (and it'll be an 11/11).

Why: Humility creates a continuous effect that applies in layer 6 ("lose all abilities") and layer 7b ("base power and toughness 1/1") [613.1]. Finale of Devastation, resolving later, grants haste in layer 6 and +10/+10 in layer 7c, and both of its effects have a later timestamp than Humility's [113.10c]. Within layer 6 the effects are applied in timestamp order: Humility strips the creature's abilities first, then Finale of Devastation adds haste afterward, so haste sticks — when two effects add and remove abilities, the most recent one prevails [113.10c]. Note Humility says "lose all abilities," not "can't have abilities," so it can't stop a later grant [113.11].

Power/toughness: layer 7b sets base 1/1 (Humility), then layer 7c adds +10/+10 (Finale of Devastation), for 11/11.

Timing detail: Finale of Devastation's ruling confirms the creature you just put onto the battlefield gets +X/+X and haste when X is 10 or more [Finale of Devastation ruling #2], and no player can act in between [Finale of Devastation ruling #0]. Humility's ability-removal applies the moment the creature is on the battlefield, so any enters-the-battlefield triggered ability it had won't trigger [603.6b] — but that doesn't affect the haste grant, which comes from outside the creature. Haste itself lets the creature attack and use {T}/untap abilities despite summoning sickness [702.10c, 302.6].

Multiplayer: the analysis is identical regardless of player count — Humility affects all creatures and Finale of Devastation affects only creatures Aitana controls; the number of opponents doesn't change the layer ordering.

(If instead Humility had entered the battlefield after Finale of Devastation resolved, Humility's layer-6 removal would be the later timestamp and the creature would lose haste.)

question: Avery's [Unlicensed Hearse] has exiled five cards, and they activate its crew ability. After that resolves, Avery casts [Dress Down]. What does Unlicensed Hearse look like?
answer:
Unlicensed Hearse becomes a colorless 0/0 Artifact Creature — Vehicle with no abilities, and it's immediately put into Avery's graveyard as a state-based action.

Why: crewing works in layer 4, making Unlicensed Hearse an artifact creature (still a Vehicle) for the turn. Dress Down's static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" applies in layer 6, and since Unlicensed Hearse is a creature at that point, it loses everything printed on it — including the characteristic-defining ability "Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness are each equal to the number of cards exiled with it." Power/toughness are set in layer 7, which is applied after layer 6, so that CDA is already gone and never sets 5/5. With no other effect defining or boosting it, Unlicensed Hearse has no P/T-defining ability at all and is 0/0. The Unlicensed Hearse ruling about crewing before exiling any cards confirms the consequence of a 0-toughness Hearse: it goes to its owner's graveyard as a state-based action unless something raises its toughness.

The five exiled cards stay in exile; they just no longer matter, because the ability that counted them (linked to the exiling ability per CR 607.1/607.2a) is gone. Losing the crew ability doesn't un-crew it — the layer 4 type change from the already-resolved crew activation continues to apply.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming crew resolved first and Dress Down resolved afterward, as stated. If instead Dress Down were already on the battlefield when Avery tried to crew, Unlicensed Hearse would have no crew ability to activate and would simply remain a non-creature artifact (and wouldn't die). Note also that Dress Down is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step — but Unlicensed Hearse will already have died long before that.

This analysis is player-count independent; nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

question: Alex controls [Karametra, God of Harvests], and then casts [Opalescence]. Their devotion to white is 2. Is Karametra, God of Harvests a creature? If so, what is its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — Karametra, God of Harvests is a creature, and it's a 5/5 (a Legendary Enchantment Creature with no creature subtype).

Why: Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability says it isn't a creature while your devotion to green and white is less than seven. Devotion to green and white counts green and white mana symbols in the mana costs of permanents you control; with only Karametra, God of Harvests ({3}{G}{W} = 2) and Opalescence ({2}{W}{W} = 2) that's 4, so the ability is active. (I'm reading "devotion to white is 2" as meaning your total devotion to green and white is well under seven; if it were seven or more, Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability simply wouldn't apply at all and Opalescence would still make it a 5/5.)

Both type-changing effects apply in layer 4 in timestamp order (CR 613.2, 613.2a for the layer-1 framing of copiable values; layer/timestamp ordering per 613.7 as referenced there):
- Layer 4, timestamp 1 (Karametra, God of Harvests entered first): Karametra, God of Harvests loses the creature type and the subtype God, becoming just a Legendary Enchantment (Karametra ruling #15).
- Layer 4, timestamp 2 (Opalescence, cast later): "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types" — Karametra, God of Harvests is now a non-Aura enchantment, so Opalescence makes it a creature again. It does not get the God subtype back.
- Layer 7b: Opalescence sets its base power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Karametra, God of Harvests' mana cost {3}{G}{W} has mana value 5, so it's 5/5, overriding the printed 6/7. Note Opalescence's setting effect applies in layer 7b regardless of what happened in layer 4 (Opalescence ruling #3 shows this layer-by-layer application).

Karametra, God of Harvests keeps indestructible and its other abilities, which function regardless of whether it's a creature (Karametra ruling #22). Because power and toughness are characteristics only creatures have (CR 302.4, 208.3), the 5/5 matters only while it's a creature — here it is one.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of players; devotion counts only permanents Alex controls, so the answer is the same at a two-player or larger table. Other permanents you control with green/white mana symbols could push devotion to seven or more, but as shown that wouldn't change the final result (still a 5/5 creature).

question: Autumn animates [Inkmoth Nexus] and attacks with it. Nayeli then flashes in [Dress Down]. What does Inkmoth Nexus look like?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus is a colorless 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature with no abilities at all, still attacking.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.6, 613.7):
- Layer 4 (types): the activated ability makes Inkmoth Nexus an artifact creature Phyrexian Blinkmoth, and "It's still a land" keeps the land type as well (CR 205.1b).
- Layer 6 (abilities), timestamp order: first Inkmoth Nexus's own effect grants flying and infect; then Dress Down's later-timestamped "Creatures lose all abilities" strips everything — flying, infect, the {T}: Add {C} mana ability, and even the {1} animation ability itself.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): even though the animating ability has been removed in layer 6, CR 613.6 says an effect that has started to apply keeps applying in every other applicable layer. So the "1/1" still applies, and Inkmoth Nexus is 1/1. (CR 613.4b; compare 208.4b on base P/T.)

Practical consequences: it stays a creature and stays attacking; it deals normal combat damage rather than infect damage, has no flying (so it can be blocked by ground creatures), and can no longer be tapped for {C}. Nothing here changes its supertypes (it has none; CR 205.4b). When Dress Down is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step, Inkmoth Nexus's abilities come back for the rest of the turn while the animation still lasts.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dress Down resolved after the animation ability resolved (which the question implies). If Dress Down had already been on the battlefield when Autumn activated the {1} ability, the result would be the same characteristics but with the timestamps reversed — Dress Down (earlier) removes abilities first, then the later animation effect grants flying and infect, which would then stick, and Inkmoth Nexus would be a 1/1 flying infect creature. Note also that Dress Down affects creatures only; if the animation had somehow ended, Inkmoth Nexus as a noncreature land would keep its abilities and have no P/T (CR 208.3).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: In their first main phase, Alexandra activates [Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance] to create two tokens, and Nehemiah responds with [Dress Down]. What happens with the tokens?
answer:
The two tokens are still created and they still have haste. Nehemiah's Dress Down doesn't stop or remove the tokens; it only strips abilities.

Sequence (assuming Dress Down was cast in response and so resolves first, on top of the Channel ability): Dress Down resolves and its static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" begins applying. Then Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's Channel ability resolves and creates two 1/1 colorless Spirit creature tokens — "create" simply means putting those tokens onto the battlefield ([Create], [111.1], [701.7c]). Nothing about Dress Down prevents a creature with those characteristics from entering, so the tokens are not stopped.

Because the same Channel ability that creates them also grants them haste until end of turn, and that grant happens after Dress Down was already on the battlefield, the tokens keep haste: per [Dress Down ruling #0], an ability granted to a creature after Dress Down has entered the battlefield is not lost (the later timestamp of the granting effect is what matters, [613.7m]). The 1/1 Spirit tokens have no other printed abilities to lose, so in practice they are unaffected — you can attack with them this turn.

If instead the order was reversed (Dress Down already resolved before you even activated Channel, or Channel resolved before Dress Down), the result is the same for these tokens: created either way, and haste granted by the Channel ability of Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance still survives, since Dress Down only removes abilities creatures have while it's applying and doesn't stop later grants. (Dress Down would only strip haste if the haste were an ability the token already had from an earlier-timestamped source.)

One side note: Dress Down's own "At the beginning of the end step, sacrifice this enchantment" is unaffected here unless something makes Dress Down a creature ([Dress Down ruling #1]).

Nothing in this answer depends on the number of players; it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

They're created as 1/1s and then gain haste. They'll be able to attack this turn.

question: Aubree casts [Blood Moon]. Nikolas activates [Inkmoth Nexus]'s ability in response. What will Inkmoth Nexus look like after everything resolves? What will it look like next turn?
answer:
Direct answer: after everything resolves, Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth Mountain artifact land creature with flying, infect, and "{T}: Add {R}" — it keeps the animation's types, 1/1 body, flying and infect, but loses its own printed "{T}: Add {C}" and "{1}: ..." abilities. Next turn (once the until-end-of-turn animation wears off) it is simply a Mountain land with "{T}: Add {R}" and nothing else, as long as Blood Moon remains on the battlefield.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1b/613.1d/613.1f, 613.3, 613.7):

- Timestamps: Nikolas's Inkmoth Nexus ability was activated in response, so it resolves first and has the earlier timestamp; Blood Moon resolves after and has the later timestamp (CR 613.7).
- Layer 4 (type-changing): Inkmoth Nexus's ability adds Artifact and Creature and the creature types Phyrexian Blinkmoth while it remains a land (CR 205.1b). Then Blood Moon sets its land subtype to Mountain. Setting a land's subtype replaces only subtypes from the land-type set (CR 205.1a), and CR 305.7 explicitly says setting a land's subtype doesn't add or remove card types such as creature, or supertypes. So it stays an artifact land creature and keeps the creature types Phyrexian Blinkmoth, now also with the land type Mountain. It is not named "Mountain" and doesn't become basic (Blood Moon ruling #1).
- Layer 6 (abilities): Inkmoth Nexus's granted flying and infect are added first (earlier timestamp). Then Blood Moon, via CR 305.7 and Blood Moon ruling #2, strips the abilities generated from the land's own rules text — "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{1}: ..." animation ability — and grants "{T}: Add {R}". CR 305.7 says this does not remove abilities that were granted by other effects, so flying and infect stay.
- Layer 7b (P/T setting): even though the animation ability itself has been removed in layer 6, CR 613.6 says an effect that has started to apply keeps applying in every other applicable layer. So the "becomes a 1/1" part still applies: 1/1.

So the resolved object: 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature (subtype also Mountain), colorless, with flying, infect, and "{T}: Add {R}".

Next turn: the animation effect has expired, so nothing adds Artifact/Creature, the creature types, flying, infect, or the 1/1 body. Blood Moon keeps applying: Inkmoth Nexus is a nonbasic land with the land type Mountain and only "{T}: Add {R}" — it cannot use "{1}" to animate again while Blood Moon is out, because that ability is removed (Blood Moon ruling #2, CR 305.7).

Timing note: this assumes Nikolas activated the ability while Blood Moon was still on the stack, as stated, so the animation resolved first. If instead Blood Moon resolved first and Nikolas tried to activate afterward, the "{1}" ability wouldn't exist to activate at all and Inkmoth Nexus would just be a Mountain-typed land with "{T}: Add {R}."

Player count doesn't matter here; the provided rules are the same for two players or a multiplayer table.

question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?
answer:
Urza's Saga is sacrificed. Once Magus of the Moon resolves and its static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies, Urza's Saga (a nonbasic land) has its land subtype set to Mountain and loses the abilities generated by its own rules text — including its chapter I, II, and III abilities and the "sacrifice after III" instruction's supporting text [305.7]. It gains the intrinsic Mountain mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6], [Mountain]. Setting a land's subtype doesn't change card types or supertypes [305.7], [205.4b], so it is still an Enchantment Land and still a Saga with lore counters on it — and a Saga with no chapter abilities remaining is immediately put into its owner's graveyard by sacrifice, exactly as [Urza's Saga ruling #1] states for Blood Moon-style effects. Niko sacrifices it as a state-based action, with no chance to use it first.

Notes:
- Type-changing effects apply in layer 4, before ability-removal is considered, which is why the Mountain-ification sticks [613.1d], [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].
- Abilities Urza's Saga already gained from resolving chapter I and chapter II ("{T}: Add {C}" and the {2}, {T} Construct-token ability) were granted by other effects, so Magus of the Moon wouldn't strip those [305.7], [Urza's Saga ruling #5] — but it doesn't matter, since Urza's Saga is sacrificed anyway.
- Magus of the Moon doesn't make it basic or rename it "Mountain" [Magus of the Moon ruling #1].
- Timing assumption: Urza's Saga is on chapter II when Magus of the Moon resolves. Nothing changes if it were on chapter I; and if Niko responds by activating the chapter II Construct ability while Magus of the Moon is still on the stack, that token is created and stays.
- This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games: Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so every opponent's and teammate's Urza's Saga is sacrificed too.

question: Nico controls [Dress Down], and Aya activates [Inkmoth Nexus]. What does it look like?
answer:
Aya's Inkmoth Nexus ends up as a 1/1 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature WITH flying and infect, even though Nico's Dress Down says "Creatures lose all abilities."

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1, 613.6):

- Layer 4 (types): Inkmoth Nexus's resolved activated ability makes it an artifact creature Phyrexian Blinkmoth that's still a land, so it keeps the Land type and gains Artifact and Creature (CR 205.1b).
- Layer 6 (abilities): Effects apply in timestamp order. Dress Down was already on the battlefield, so its "Creatures lose all abilities" (timestamp earlier) applies first and strips everything Inkmoth Nexus had \u2014 including its {T}: Add {C} mana ability and the {1} animation ability itself. Then the Inkmoth Nexus effect, with the later timestamp (created when the ability resolved), applies its "with flying and infect" part and grants those two abilities back. Per CR 613.6, once an effect starts applying in one layer (layer 4 here) it keeps applying in every other applicable layer even if the ability that generated it is removed in the meantime \u2014 so losing the {1} ability in layer 6 does not undo the rest of the already-resolved effect.
- Layer 7b (P/T): The same effect sets power and toughness to 1/1.

Net result: a 1/1 flying, infect land artifact creature named Inkmoth Nexus, colorless, with no mana ability and no way to activate the {1} animation again while Dress Down is out (any further activation would have to come from an untouched copy of the ability \u2014 it's been removed, so Aya can't activate it again).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dress Down was already on the battlefield when Aya activated Inkmoth Nexus (as stated). If instead Nico flashed in Dress Down *after* the Inkmoth Nexus ability resolved, Dress Down would have the later timestamp, would apply second in layer 6, and would strip flying and infect \u2014 leaving a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature with no abilities (still 1/1, since the P/T-setting part is layer 7b and unaffected).

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players.

question: Ariana controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue." Nico casts [Dress Down]. What color are Painter's Servant and Dress Down?
answer:
Both are blue. Painter's Servant is blue (and no longer colorless), and Dress Down is blue.

Why Painter's Servant is blue: color-changing effects are applied in layer 5, and ability-adding/removing effects are applied in layer 6, which comes *after* layer 5. So when the game applies layer 5, Painter's Servant still has its ability "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color in addition to their other colors," and that effect makes every permanent — including Painter's Servant itself and Dress Down — blue. Only afterward, in layer 6, does Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" strip Painter's Servant's abilities; that removal happens too late to undo the color change already applied (CR 613.6 confirms an effect that has started to apply keeps applying even if its source ability is removed).

Details:
- Painter's Servant's printed mana cost is {2} (all generic), so it has no colored mana symbols and is normally colorless [202.2b, 105.2c]. Because a normally colorless object just becomes the new color rather than being both blue and colorless [Painter's Servant ruling #0], Painter's Servant ends up mono-blue, a 1/3 Artifact Creature — Scarecrow with no abilities.
- Dress Down's cost is {1}{U}, so it is already blue from its mana cost [202.2, 202.2b]. Painter's Servant's effect adds blue, which it already is [Painter's Servant ruling #5], so Dress Down is simply blue. Dress Down is an Enchantment, not a creature, so its own "Creatures lose all abilities" never touches its own abilities.
- Colorless is not a color [Colorless, 105.1], so "colorless" isn't something Painter's Servant keeps alongside blue.

Timing note: I'm assuming Dress Down has resolved and is on the battlefield. While Dress Down is still on the stack, nothing has lost abilities yet, and the answer is the same colors anyway (Painter's Servant blue, Dress Down blue) since Painter's Servant's ability also colors spells.

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games — Painter's Servant affects all permanents and spells regardless of controller, so Nico's Dress Down is blue even though Ariana controls Painter's Servant.

question: Anabella controls [Blood Moon] and enchants their [Sunlit Marsh] with [Urban Utopia]. What colors can it tap for?
answer:
Sunlit Marsh can tap for any one color — {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} — thanks to Urban Utopia, plus it separately has "{T}: Add {R}" from being a Mountain. (Each tap uses one of those abilities, so one tap yields one mana of whatever color you choose.)

Why: Sunlit Marsh is a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" sets its subtype to Mountain. Under CR 305.7, setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose its old land types and all abilities generated from its rules text and old types — so Sunlit Marsh loses "{T}: Add {W} or {B}" — and it gains the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6, Mountain entry; Blood Moon ruling #2). Blood Moon does not change its name or supertypes (Blood Moon ruling #1).

Crucially, CR 305.7 also says this does not remove abilities that were granted to the land by other effects. Urban Utopia grants "Enchanted land has '{T}: Add one mana of any color'" as a separate continuous effect, so that ability sticks around regardless of the order in which Blood Moon and Urban Utopia started applying (Urban Utopia ruling #0 confirms the enchanted land doesn't lose other abilities or change land types). question: Avery enchants their [Hall] with [Unbridled Growth]. Next turn, Nickolas casts [Blood Moon]. What colors of mana can Hall tap for?
answer:
Hall can still tap for any one color: white, blue, black, red, or green.

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," which sets Hall's land subtype to Mountain. Under CR 305.7, setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose the abilities generated from its own rules text and its old land types (so Hall loses "This land enters tapped," "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and "{4}, {T}: Investigate") and gain the intrinsic Mountain mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6, Mountain, Blood Moon ruling #2). But CR 305.7 explicitly says this "doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects." Unbridled Growth grants an ability ("Enchanted land has '{T}: Add one mana of any color'") rather than defining a characteristic (CR 113.12), and it comes from a separate permanent, so it survives Blood Moon.

Working it through the layer system (CR 613.9): in layer 4 Hall becomes a Mountain; in layer 6 Unbridled Growth's granted ability is added (earlier timestamp), Blood Moon strips Hall's own printed abilities, and the Mountain intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" is added. End result: Hall is a land with subtype Mountain whose only abilities are "{T}: Add one mana of any color" and "{T}: Add {R}." Tapping it once produces one mana of whatever color Avery chooses (the {R}-only ability is strictly worse but also available). Note Hall loses "enters tapped" and the Investigate ability while Blood Moon is on the battlefield.

Timestamp note: it doesn't matter here whether Unbridled Growth or Blood Moon arrived first — CR 305.7's carve-out for granted abilities applies either way. If Unbridled Growth leaves the battlefield, Hall is left with only "{T}: Add {R}."

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.
